newsitem.title: UK: Guinness, G. Met raise hopes for solution.
newsitem.headline: Guinness, G. Met raise hopes for solution.

text.p: British drinks group Guinness Plc said on Friday it hoped a solution could be found to its increasingly bitter row with France's LVMH over Guinness' attempted merger with Grand Metropolitan Plc.

"I very much hope there is a solution here. I think we have clearly talked about the criteria and we have already seen a degree of shifting on his part. You will notice he is no longer talking about 35 percent," Guinness chairman Tony Greener told a news conference, referring to LVMH chief Bernard Arnault.

Executives of both Guinness and Grand Met, who proposed in May to merge to create a 24 billion stg company, GMG Brands, stressed that including LVMH's drinks arm Moet Hennessy, as Arnault has proposed, would improve the merger but it would have to be at a price which created value for shareholders.
"It is entirely in character that he would start with a very high demand," said Greener.

Arnault is seeking to include LVMH's drinks arm Moet Hennessy in a three-way merger with Guinness' United Distillers and Grand Met's IDV. He wants to name the group DrinksCo with a separate listing in Paris and London and take a 35 percent shareholding.
John McGrath, chief executive of Grand Met, told reporters if LVMH took 35 percent it would mean an inequitable shift in profits of 130 million stg a year away from GMG Brands shareholders.
Arnault also wants GMG Brands to demerge fast food chain Burger King, Guinness brewing and U.S. food producer Pillsbury.
Grand Met and Guinness said in a statement earlier today the demerger proposal "would result in a substantial loss of shareholder value for the GMG Brands shareholders other than LVMH."
In the statement, the two British firms also said the plan would result in a loss of value of 1.5 billion pounds and possibly "significantly more."
McGrath said in the case of Burger King, the company had commissioned exhaustive studies by advisers and not a single bank had come up with a way round the onerous tax costs of a demerger.
But he said the companies were open-minded about demerger, "and we cannot get across to Mr Arnault, who thinks that we are opposed to it because he suggested it."
He said management would be impeded if one shareholder took as substantial a stake as Arnault was suggesting along with a senior management role.
George Bull, chairman of Grand Met, described the problem as "a bit like the old tail wagging the dog."

He said that IDV is already the world's largest spirits company and UD is number two, whereas if they involved Moet Hennessy brands, it would increase spirits portfolio by three percent and the wine portfolio by six percent.
"They are tiny amounts in relationship to what we are talking about," Bull said.

LVMH has dismissed the objections raised by Guinness and Grand Met, claiming they added "nothing of value to the situation," and said the plans to merge as GMG Brands were a "short-term, incomplete solution."
Greener said it was the task of Guinness and Grand Met to make sure that Arnault understood what the two British companies would find acceptable.
"This is going to be a very long running affair and to do a quick deal with LVMH will be very expensive for Guinness and Grand Met shareholders," Greener added.
